title: Death comes even if we haven't practiced
word: Death comes even if we haven't practiced
hookLine: the to-do list from January is still open; the Dhammapada's old herons, and the moon out of the clouds
tomorrow: a girl answered the Buddha 'i don't know.' why was she right?

lines: WHAT IF TIME RUNS OUT FIRST?
cards: Somewhere there's a list from January: learn the guitar, call more, start meditating. Some of it is still open. What if the time runs out before you've started?
The Buddhist answer has two halves, and they come from the same little book, the Dhammapada. The first half stings. The second one lets the light back in.

teach.h: OLD HERONS AT AN EMPTY LAKE.

teach.b: The Dhammapada pictures people who let their young years go without practice and without building anything: they waste away like old herons at a lake with no fish, or lie like worn-out bows, sighing over the past.
Time passes whether or not it's used. Death doesn't wait for the practice to start. Second half, a few verses later.

teach.h: THE MOON OUT OF THE CLOUDS.
teach.b: Whoever was heedless before and later wakes up lights up the world, like the moon slipping out of the clouds. Not too late. Never too late while there's breath.
Both halves are true at once, and that's the week. It opened at a sickbed, where Nakula's mother showed practice is everywhere. Then why reflect on death at all: to live well.
One mouthful, one breath more. Dusk and dawn, ending in effort or in gladness. Atisha's first root: death is certain.
And today, the sting and the moon: time passes, so start.

how: Buddhist teachers often pair the Dhammapada's warning verses with its verse of the moon freed from clouds, so that reflection on lost time leads to starting again rather than to regret.

games.q: what does “death comes even if we haven't practiced” mean?
o: death won't wait for you to begin practicing
a rule that only lifelong monks reach the goal
a belief that practice can stop death coming

games.q: the two halves — tap the pairs.
p: the moon out of the clouds

s: in the Dhammapada, once your young years are gone, it's too late to practice
whoever was heedless and later wakes up lights up the world, like the moon out of the clouds.
the Dhammapada compares wasted years to old herons at a lake with no fish
and to worn-out bows, sighing over the past.

games.q: your uncle says he's too old to start meditating: 'that ship sailed.' which half of today's Dhammapada answers him?
o: the herons: if the young years are gone, it's gone.
the moon: whoever wakes up later still lights up the world.
neither: the Dhammapada is only about monks.
games.why: time passes, and the herons sting. but the moon slips out of the clouds for whoever wakes up, whenever they wake.

practice: Choose ten minutes from later today and name the one thing that's been waiting for them. Name what usually eats those minutes, the phone, the couch, the doubt.
Then decide quietly: when that happens, I'll start anyway, and rest with that plan until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Death comes even if we haven't practiced: time doesn't wait for a start. And the moon can still come out.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: time; the thing that passes whether or not it's used.

carryVoice: Your line: time passes, and the moon can still come out of the clouds. A week of remembering, done. Day sixteen thirty-one.

sources.ref: Dhammapada 155-156 (the old herons at a lake without fish; the worn-out bows sighing over the past)
Dhammapada 172 (the one who was heedless and later is heedful brightens the world like the moon freed from clouds)
